# Jev models make agents faster. Hooked control planes steal the difference.

A five-layer hook chain keeps a tenth of what system-one judgment earns, no matter how fast the next model gets.

Kendall Clark · Pentad Labs · 14 October 2026 · PLRN-031

## Abstract

In August 2026 a frontier model call took seconds, and a control check that cost a few hundred milliseconds was noise beside it. By October, small classifiers make many of the same judgments in tens of milliseconds.

But the control stack that enterprises assemble for agents didn’t get faster at all. It’s often acquired as five layers from five separate vendors (runtime, control, observability, governance, and orchestration) and joined by hooks, which are network calls. A model of that chain built from published network and vendor latencies gives a median of 115 ms when every vendor runs in the customer’s cloud region and 450 ms when they are reached as public SaaS, with p99s of 318 ms and 993 ms.

In both cases the check costs more than the judgment it checks. This note calls that the crossover.

Crossover matters because agents got faster. An agent that sends some of its turns to fast calls finishes sooner, and a fixed control cost on every turn then behaves as the serial fraction in Amdahl’s law. A fixed control cost caps the speedup that faster judgment can deliver and claims a growing share of the agent’s time as more turns go faster.

A public-SaaS hook chain keeps about 10% of the speedup that in-path control allows, however slow the frontier call it replaces: moving every turn from a 60s call to a 50 ms call yields 121-fold rather than 1,200-fold. Making the fast call ten times faster again moves that ceiling only from 121 to 133. The cost falls on the agents whose engineers moved the most judgment off the frontier model, which is a perversion of incentives.

This note argues that

- a control decision has to complete inside the time-envelope of the action it governs. After the crossover a five-layer stack can’t meet that condition, physically.

- latency is the lesser half of the problem. The controls worth having join data that the five layers hold separately, and in a five-layer stack those joins aren’t slow, they’re just never built. In some sense, they are NaN-slower.

- an integrated platform can make the joins, but few if any of them will host their competitors’ agents.

Speed in the path of the action, one place that holds all the state, and neutrality among vendors are therefore jointly required, and no existing arrangement provides all three.

## TLDR

- While agent judgment took seconds, control could take hundreds of milliseconds without anyone minding. (§1)

- Small classifiers now make in-turn judgments in tens of milliseconds, so control has a budget it didn’t have before. (§2)

- A chain of five hooked layers costs about 115 ms at the median in region and about 450 ms over public SaaS, and its tail compounds with every layer. (§3)

- Agents that route some of their turns to fast calls are faster, and a fixed control cost per turn is the serial fraction in Amdahl’s sense. A public-SaaS hook chain keeps about a tenth of the available speedup, however slow the frontier call, and faster judgment beyond that point buys almost nothing. The cost lands on the agents with the most fast turns. (§4)

- The per-turn crossover is past. The fleet crossover has two thresholds. At 50% fast turns a governed agent’s median turn is mostly control, under no assumption beyond the measured latencies. Its wall time tips at a fast-turn share set by the slow call: 99.3% at 60 s, 58% at 1 s. Dates follow only from an assumed routing path: a cohort going from 90% to 99% fast turns in a year crosses the public-SaaS chain at the end of 2027 and the in-region chain in mid-2028, and a year later if the climb takes two. The stack is turned off before it is replaced. (§5)

- A check that returns after the act is a record of the act, not a control over it. To govern, a control must be invoked on the path of the action, finish before the action’s effect, and take a small fraction of the action’s own time . (§6)

- The most valuable controls need data from several layers at once. In a five-layer stack those joins don’t arrive late. They don’t exist. (§7)

- An integrated platform can make the joins but can’t be neutral among vendors’ agents. The requirement is the conjunction: in the path, unified, and neutral. (§8)

## 1. Agent controls aren’t cheap any more

Until recently an agent’s turn was dominated by its model call. Frontier calls are slow and their distribution is long-tailed. Across all traffic through its gateway in April 2026, Requesty measured a p50 end-to-end latency of 5.8 s and a p95 of 52.6 s for Anthropic, 2.5 s and 17.9 s for OpenAI, and 13.7 s and 115.2 s for Claude on Vertex, a tail it attributes mainly to agentic coding workloads.

Those figures include trivial calls. A measured distribution sharpens them: across 665,453 Claude Code and Codex calls logged in TraceLab v0.0.2, the per-call p10 is 1.9 s and the median 6.3 s, and calls that carry substantive generation are slower: a median of 27.9 s for calls producing a thousand or more output tokens, 46.7 s at two thousand or more, with p95 at 108 to 147 s and p99 past 280 s (Zhu et al. 2026). The calls that dominate an agent’s elapsed time sit in the tens of seconds to minutes, which is consistent with the measured tails and with Artificial Analysis’s reports of complete responses measured in minutes for the highest-effort configurations. Against a call of that length, a guardrail service that added two or three hundred milliseconds changed nothing a user could notice.

Practitioners have a rule for when that stops being true. O’Connor, reporting on six guardrail tools run inline on a production agent, puts it as follows: inline checks past about 50 ms are felt by users, and past about 200 ms someone turns them off during an incident . The rule was rarely tested while the model call dwarfed everything around it.

So the hook is the dominant integration pattern for agent control:

- Each layer exposes a callback, and

- the agent or its harness calls it before or after a step: to ask whether a tool call is allowed, to log what happened, to charge a budget, to check an output.

- in the limit case, each layer is a separate product, usually from a separate vendor, reached over a network.

The dominant pattern was reasonable because it was cheap relative to what it controlled.

## 2. Judgment got fast

The judgments that control depends on are narrow. Is this input an injection? Does this output contain personal data? Is this tool call within the task’s scope? None of them requires a frontier model, and in September 2026 a class of model built for exactly this shape of question arrived. TypeSafe AI’s Jev, released on 15 September, returns a typed decision, a choice among options, a score, or a yes or no, rather than text, and its vendor claims it answers such questions “40x-200x faster for the same levels of frontier intelligence” (Almeida 2026). The vendor’s end-to-end figure is 70 to 500 ms, measured from laptops on the West Coast, with no percentiles. Three weeks later a16z, announcing its investment, reported a trillion tokens served in the first three days and a quarter of the Fortune 500 integrated, and named the effect: “make intelligence cheap enough to call anywhere, and it gets called everywhere” (Andreessen Horowitz 2026).

Independent measurement followed within the week. this-that-model-1.0, an open 2B-parameter decision model, makes a decision in 30.9 ms on one laptop GPU against 8,758 ms for the frontier call it replaces (Cheng, Dai, and Sun 2026). A survey of public GitHub projects counted 2,170 that called Jev by 22 September (Ling, Xue, and Ye 2026). REFLEX puts a system-one model in front of the strong model as a selective control layer and removes 72.7% of strong-model calls at 95% task success (Wu and Lim 2026). The questions control asks are the questions these models answer.

The fast tier existed before September in narrower form. Meta’s model card for Prompt Guard 2 reports 19.3 ms per classification for the 22M model and 92.4 ms for the 86M model, on an A100 with 512-token inputs, and vendor summaries describe the same tiers more loosely: single-digit milliseconds for pattern checks, tens of milliseconds for small classifiers, and hundreds of milliseconds to seconds for a judge model that rereads the context. Those summaries publish no method, and this note uses them only as a description of tiers. What changed in September is that the fast tier stopped being a set of special-purpose classifiers and became a general interface, and engineers began routing judgment through it.

WunderOS’s own in-path scorer is a model of this class. It’s the neural model that decides what the context window keeps ( PLRN-022 ), and it measures 89 ms on a fresh input and 12 µs on a cached one. The admission decision, the control gate every piece of work passes before it starts, measures 142 µs at p99. Both are measured on master; the run identifiers are in the method note.

The fast call this note models, \(J_f\) = 50 ms in §4, is an open system-one model served in the customer’s region or on the box, not the hosted endpoint. A decision fetched over the public internet costs what §3 charges for one hook, and the one public Jev-backed tool gate for a coding agent, pi-jev, reports about 300 ms per round trip. No independent percentile for the hosted service has been published, and this note quotes none.

Figure 1 shows what follows. The cost of a judgment, as measured in latency bands, fell by about two orders of magnitude between August and October, and most of it came in September. The control around it stayed where it was.

## 3. What a hook chain costs

The figure’s orange band is a model, and the model is stated here so that it can be checked and replaced with a measurement.

The chain. A governed action passes through up to five layers.

- Each layer is a separate service, and each call costs one network round trip plus the service’s own processing.

- The calls run in sequence, because each layer needs the previous layer’s output: governance needs the grant that control resolved, and the record needs both.

- A final step correlates the five answers, which share no common run or grant identifier. Every component is drawn from a lognormal distribution, the usual shape for service latency.

The parameters.

- For vendors deployed in the customer’s region, the round-trip median is 1.5 ms, which is the cross-zone p50 that AWS reports from ping tests in three regions (Haken).

- For vendors reached as public SaaS, it is 30 ms, an assumption.

- Processing has a median of 15 ms in region and 40 ms over SaaS, with a p99 eight times the median.

The SaaS figure is anchored to Lakera’s published p95 for its SaaS endpoint: under 20 ms for a 1,000-character input, 100–200 ms at 10,000 characters, and 300–400 ms at 30,000. An agent’s turn, with its tool results and history, commonly runs past 10,000 characters, so 40 ms is a conservative median for a check that reads it. Correlation costs 5 ms in region and 10 ms over SaaS, which are very generous estimates.
